title: Reported speech
intro: This last unit of B1 is about passing on words. You can quote someone exactly: *“Gijä galdym” diýdi*. You can link a quote or a thought to another verb with *diýip*: *“Nirede?” diýip sorady*, *Ýagyş ýagar diýip pikir etdim*. The same *diýip* after a wish says **so that**: *Çaga oýanmasyn diýip ýuwaş gürledik*. And you can report without quoting, with the fact clauses of [B1 unit 6](b1-u06) and the verbal nouns of [B1 unit 4](b1-u04): *Ertir geljekdigini aýtdy*, *Meniň gelmegimi haýyş etdi*.

blocks.text: *Diýmek* introduces someone's exact words. The quote comes first, in quotation marks, and the verb follows it: *“Men gijä galdym” diýdi*, he said, “I'm late.” *Aýtmak* is **to say, to tell**; it takes what is said as its object, and the person told in the dative: *Ol maňa hakykaty aýtdy*, she told me the truth.

To name the speaker before the quote, put a colon after them: *Ol maňa: “Ertir gel” diýdi*, she said to me, “Come tomorrow.” The speaker can also come right before the quote with no verb after it: *Ejem sorady: “Nirä barýarsyň?”*. Other verbs of speaking work the same way: *soramak* (to ask, with the person asked in the ablative: *mugallymdan sorady*), *jogap bermek* (to answer, with the person or question in the dative), *gygyrmak* (to shout).

The verb of saying comes straight after the closing quotation mark, with no comma. A question mark or an exclamation mark stays inside the quote: *“Gel!” diýdi*. In books you will also see « » and a dash before the verb: *«Gel!» – diýdi*. This course writes “ ”.

items.en: “I'm late,” he said.
She said to me, “Come tomorrow.”
The teacher said, “Open your books.”
My mum asked, “Where are you going?”
She told me the truth.
I answered her question.

blocks.title: Diýmek also means and calls
blocks.text: *Diýmek* is also **to mean** and **to call**: *Bu söz näme diýmek?* (what does this word mean?), *Oňa Batyr diýýärler* (they call him Batyr). Its present has two *ý*: *diýýär*, *diýýärin*.

blocks.title: Keep the speaker's own words
blocks.text: Inside the quote, keep the speaker's person and tense: *Aýna: “Men ýadaw” diýdi*, Aýna said she was tired. The *men* is Aýna, not you. And *aýtmak* tells a person something, *diýmek* quotes: *Ol maňa hiç zat aýtmady*, he didn't tell me anything.

*Diýip* is the converb of *diýmek*, literally **saying**. It links a quote to another verb: *“Gijä galdym” diýip ylgady*, “I'm late,” he said, and ran off. *“Nirede?” diýip sorady*, she asked, “Where?” With *aýtmak*, *soramak*, *jogap bermek* and *gygyrmak*, a quote is usually followed by *diýip*: *Men oňa “Gelmerin” diýip aýtdym*, I told him I wouldn't come.

*Diýip* also introduces what someone thinks, hopes or fears, in the words they would think it: *Ýagyş ýagar diýip pikir etdim*, I thought it would rain, literally “it will rain,” I thought. The tense stays as it was thought. With *öýtmek* (to think, to suppose) the thought comes straight before the verb, with no *diýip*: *Ol geler öýdýärin*, I think she'll come; *Ol dogry aýdýar öýdýärin*, I think he's right.
And *diýip* names things: *Ogluna Batyr diýip at dakdylar*, they named their son Batyr. The participle *diýen* means **called**: *Kemine diýen şahyr*, a poet called Kemine.

items.en: “I'm late,” he said, and ran off.
“Where are you going?” she asked.
I told him I wouldn't come.
I thought it would rain.
I think she'll come.
They named their son Batyr.

blocks.title: *öýtmek* (to think, to suppose), present: I think…
öýdýärin: t becomes d
blocks.text: *Öýtmek* is one of the verbs whose *t* softens before a vowel and before *-ýär*, like *gitmek*: *öýdýärin*, *öýdüp*, but *öýtdüm*, *öýtjek*. Its past is *öýtdüm*, **I thought**: *Ol geler öýtdüm*, I thought she'd come.

blocks.title: Two verbs of saying in a row
blocks.text: When a quote goes with *sorady*, *aýtdy*, *gygyrdy* or *jogap berdi*, link it with *diýip*, not *diýdi*: *“Hawa” diýip jogap berdi*, not `“Hawa” diýdi jogap berdi`.

sections.title: diýip for so that and because

blocks.text: Put a wish before *diýip* and it gives the purpose of an action, often for someone else: *Çaga oýanmasyn diýip ýuwaş gürledik*, we spoke quietly so that the baby wouldn't wake up, literally saying “let the baby not wake.” The wish takes the forms of [A2 unit 7](a2-u07): `-sYn` for him, her or them, `-AýYn` for me, `-AlY` for us, and their negatives for **so that … not**.

Before *diýip* a thought can also give the reason for what you did: *Gijä galaryn diýip ylgadym*, I ran because I thought I'd be late. *Myhmanlar aç bolandyr diýip nahar taýýarladym*, I made some food, thinking the guests would be hungry.

Compare `-mAk üçin` from [B1 unit 4](b1-u04): *Wagtynda ýetmek üçin ir çykdyk*. When the purpose is your own action, both are fine. When it is someone else's, use the wish and *diýip*: *Çagalar görmesin diýip sowgady gizledim*, I hid the present so that the children wouldn't see it.

items.en: We talked quietly so that the baby wouldn't wake up.

items.tk: Gijä galmaýyn diýip taksi bilen gitdim.
items.seg: Gijä gal|ma|ýyn diý|ip taksi bilen gitdim.
items.en: I took a taxi so as not to be late.

items.tk: Hemme kişi eşitsin diýip gaty gürledi.
items.seg: Hemme kişi eşit|sin diý|ip gaty gürledi.
items.en: He spoke loudly so that everyone could hear.
I hid the present so that the children wouldn't see it.
I dressed warmly so that I wouldn't catch a cold.
I ran because I thought I'd be late.

blocks.title: A wish, not a prediction
blocks.text: For **so that … not**, the wish is negative: *oýanmasyn*, *galmaýyn*. *Oýanmaz diýip* would be a thought, **thinking he won't wake up**, which is a reason, not a purpose.

To report a statement without quoting it, make it a fact clause with `-dYgY` ([B1 unit 6](b1-u06)) and the accusative, before *aýtmak*: *“Ertir gelerin”* → *Ol ertir geljekdigini aýtdy*, he said he would come tomorrow. The possessive shows whose statement it is: *geljekdigimi* (that I would come), *geljekdigiňi* (that you would come), *geljekdigini* (that he or she would come). To make clear the speaker means himself, add *özüniň*: *Ol özüniň geljekdigini aýtdy*.

The tense stays as it was said; Turkmen doesn't shift it back as English does. Aýna said *“Men ýadaw”*, so *Aýna ýadawdygyny aýtdy*, Aýna said she **was** tired. Merdan said *“Aşgabatda ýaşaýaryn”*, so *Merdan Aşgabatda ýaşaýandygyny aýtdy*, he said he **lived** in Ashgabat.

blocks.caption: From quote to report

Reported
Meaning
rows: He said he lived in Ashgabat.
She said she had seen him.
He said he would come tomorrow.

blocks.text: To report a question, keep its question word inside the clause and use *soramak*: *“Nirä gidýärsiň?”* → *Ol meniň nirä gidýändigimi sorady*, he asked where I was going; *Men ondan haçan geljekdigini soradym*, I asked her when she would come. A yes-or-no question is easiest to quote with *diýip*: *Ol maňa “Gelersiňmi?” diýip sorady*.

To report a request or an order, use the verbal noun `-mAk` with the possessive and the accusative ([B1 unit 4](b1-u04)), before *haýyş etmek* (to ask, to request), *aýtmak* (to tell) or *buýurmak* (to order): *“Gel!”* → *Ol meniň gelmegimi haýyş etdi*, she asked me to come. *Ejem maňa ir gelmegimi aýtdy*, mum told me to come early. The person asked is in the ablative with *haýyş etmek*: *Men ondan kömek etmegini haýyş etdim*, I asked him to help.

items.en: He said he would come tomorrow.
Aýna said she was tired.
He asked where I was going.
She asked me to come.

items.tk: Men ondan kömek etmegini haýyş etdim.
items.seg: Men ondan kömek et|meg|i|n|i haýyş etdim.
items.en: I asked him to help.
The teacher told us to open our books.

blocks.title: Or keep the words
blocks.text: You can also keep the original words with *diýdi*, changing nothing: *Ol “Ertir gelerin” diýdi*, he said he would come tomorrow. Both ways are correct; with `-dYgY` you change the person, with *diýdi* you keep it.

blocks.title: soramak for questions
blocks.text: A reported question takes *soramak*, not *aýtmak*: *Nirede ýaşaýandygymy sorady*, he asked where I lived. *Nirede ýaşaýandygymy aýtdy* would mean that he told someone where I lived.

lines.en: She said there would be an exam tomorrow.
Really? Did she say when it would start?

lines.tk: Hawa, sagat dokuzda. Ol bize ir gelmegimizi haýyş etdi.
lines.en: Yes, at nine. She asked us to come early.

lines.tk: Men kitabymy mekdepde galdyrdym. Okamaga wagtym ýok öýdýärin.
lines.en: I left my book at school. I don't think I have time to study.

lines.tk: Alada etme. Saňa gerek bolar diýip, depderimi getirdim.
lines.en: Don't worry. I brought my notebook, thinking you'd need it.

lines.tk: Sag bol! Sen iň gowy dost!

summary: *Diýmek* follows a quote: *“Gijä galdym” diýdi*. Put a colon after a speaker named first: *Ol maňa: “Gel” diýdi*. No comma before *diýdi*.
*Aýtmak* tells something to someone (dative): *Ol maňa hakykaty aýtdy*. *Soramak* asks someone (ablative): *mugallymdan sorady*.
*Diýip* links a quote or a thought to another verb: *“Nirede?” diýip sorady*; *Ýagyş ýagar diýip pikir etdim*. *Öýtmek* takes the thought directly: *Ol geler öýdýärin*.
A wish with *diýip* gives a purpose: *Çaga oýanmasyn diýip ýuwaş gürledik*; *Gijä galmaýyn diýip …*
Statements are reported with `-dYgY` + possessive + accusative before *aýtmak*: *geljekdigini aýtdy*. The tense doesn't shift back.
Questions keep their question word and take *soramak*: *nirä gidýändigimi sorady*.
Requests take the verbal noun with the possessive: *gelmegimi haýyş etdi*, *ir gelmegimi aýtdy*.
